absent: Behavior of positional and non-positional vector helpers and offset construction from halves.
Internals of range verification, generic read-write checks, limit enforcement and write fencing.
Pipe allocation, splice intake, buffer release, wait queue, wakeup and signal primitives beyond observed calls.
File operation callbacks for copy, remap, iterate and splice completion including their locking.
User-memory copy, compatibility detection, security permission and container helper internals.
Accounting, notification, access-time and size-read effects beyond invocation.
Numeric values of ceilings, maxima, flags, modes and error codes beyond their roles.
Full layouts of inode, file, pipe, iterator and traversal context beyond fields shown.
Position update and fault precedence on zero or negative completion.
Concurrency ordering between directory readers and writers beyond lock use.

findings.text: Flagless positional vector entries accept a descriptor, user vector with length, and explicit offset, delegating to internal positional vector logic with no additional behavior flags. Native forms rebuild the offset from low and high halves, while compatibility forms either accept a wide offset directly or synthesize it from paired halves.

Flagged positional vector entries add a behavior word and interpret an all-ones offset as a request for the current position. On that sentinel they use the non-positional vector path with caller flags, otherwise they use the positional vector path with the given offset and flags.
Compatibility offset synthesis preserves 64-bit positioning by placing the high half above the low half, giving split-word entries the same explicit-offset meaning as wide-offset entries.

Sendfile setup requires resolvable descriptors, read ability on the source and write ability on the destination, derives the source position from its current location when no pointer is supplied and otherwise from caller storage with an extra positioned-read requirement, then validates the source range before transfer.

Sendfile length control applies a global ceiling and filesystem maxima, defaulting an absent ceiling to the smaller of the two filesystem limits, narrowing or rejecting requests that would cross the ceiling, and rechecking ceiling violation after completion.

Sendfile completion policy selects direct file-to-file movement for ordinary destinations and file-to-pipe movement for pipe destinations with nonblocking propagated only there, and after a positive transfer records accounting, emits access and modification events, advances the destination location, updates either caller storage or the source location, and counts the operation.

Direct splice movement is offered to kernel callers for copying a length between files at explicit positions. The outer form fixes the consume routine, while the inner form packages length, flags, source position, destination object, completion callback and destination position reference, rejects destinations without write ability or with append mode, runs the shared engine, and publishes the new source position on success.

The direct engine demands a seekable source, reuses a task-held pipe or allocates one with a single reader, keeps output draining while retaining caller blocking choice for input, and requires the pipe to start empty. It cycles through chunk intake, consumer execution, and progress accounting, manages a more-data hint around sufficiency, triggers end handling only after partial progress on terminal empty intake without an initial hint, frees residual pipe content on short or failed runs, resets indices, marks source access, and reports total moved or terminal status.

Movement into a pipe holds the destination pipe lock across readiness waiting and content insertion, releasing before any reader notification, so queue state changes are atomic to concurrent pipe users.

Pipe space waiting reports a broken pipe with signal delivery when readers are gone, succeeds at once when room exists, and otherwise returns a retryable status for nonblocking callers, a restart status when signals await, or sleeps for writability.
Reader notification orders prior queue changes before observing waiter presence, wakes interruptible waiters when any exist, and always issues asynchronous poll signalling to registered readers.

Sendfile entries move bytes from an input descriptor to an output descriptor with optional caller offset storage. Absent storage uses current positions, present storage is fetched from user memory and used as the source position with a ceiling that is restricted for plain forms and unrestricted for 64-bit forms, then written back. Fetch or writeback faults are reported as memory faults.

Copy validation enforces mount policy by permitting cross-mount splice, demanding identical offload handlers when the destination offloads, and otherwise demanding a shared mount. It refuses immutable destinations and swap participants, rejects wrapping offsets, shortens to source end, applies destination limits, refuses self-overlap within one inode, and returns the adjusted length.

Kernel copy-range service accepts only a splice hint, validates and verifies both ranges, completes empty requests at once, clamps length for splice, non-offload, or compatibility callers, then prefers destination offload, then same-mount remap with shortening and splice fallback, then same-mount splice, dropping the destination write guard before splice to avoid cross-mount deadlock, and reports notifications and accounting on success.

Copy-range entry resolves both descriptors, obtains positions from caller storage when supplied else from current locations, rejects any nonzero flag word, delegates to the kernel copy service, and on success advances both positions to caller storage or current locations, mapping writeback failures to faults.

Generic write checks refuse swap targets, accept empty length immediately, move append-mode position to current size, refuse nonblocking waits without direct or async-write support, enforce destination limits with possible shortening, and restrict the caller iterator to the approved amount.
Atomic write checks demand a linear user buffer, power-of-two length, position alignment to that length, and direct mode, distinguishing shape errors from unsupported non-direct use.

Directory traversal normally uses shared inode ownership acquired in killable form and bypasses locking for immutable content. A wrapper for legacy filesystems releases shared ownership, takes exclusive ownership, rechecks liveness after the gap, runs the supplied iterator, then downgrades to shared before returning.

Shared directory traversal requires an available iterator plus read allowance from security and notification controls, rejects dead directories, carries file position into and out of caller context, and on success produces access events and access-time update before releasing shared ownership.
Permission notification for files has two configurations: one evaluates area-based permission with no range, the other unconditionally grants.
Directory name emission to user memory terminates the destination after the name length and then transfers the name bytes.

Legacy entry layout holds inode number and offset in native words, name length in a short, and a trailing flexible name. Its footprint is measured as the offset of the name member at a chosen length. Callback state for single-entry reads pairs traversal context with a user entry pointer and a numeric outcome.

Legacy entry filling allows a single success, validates positive bounded length without separators, rejects inode values that narrow on conversion, counts the entry, transfers number, offset, length and terminated name to user space, maps user faults to fault status, and stops once an outcome exists.

Legacy directory read resolves the descriptor with position safety, requests a one-entry hint with a user buffer, runs shared traversal, favors the fill outcome when present, and returns the final status.

Directory and write validation helpers are provided for filesystem use, covering shared traversal, exclusive-conversion wrapping, generic limit enforcement with iterator adjustment, counted write validation, and atomic shape validation.

Observed limits and sentinels: all-ones offset means current position; vector and copy lengths observe a global ceiling; plain sendfile observes a non-large-file ceiling while 64-bit forms use filesystem maxima; copies shorten to source end; names must be positive, below path maximum, and separator-free; atomic writes use power-of-two aligned lengths.

Observed modes and outcomes: read, write, positioned-read and seek abilities gate movement; append forbids direct splice and repositions writes; nonblocking feeds splice behavior on pipe paths; more-data hint is managed internally; copy allows only a splice hint with optional remap shortening; direct and async-write gate nonblocking; immutable skips directory locks; checks use read intent; failures distinguish descriptor, pipe, overflow, cross-device, busy, argument, permission and fault cases.

Hazards include narrowed inode numbers on some builds, user-memory faults on offset or entry transfer, position-plus-length overflow past ceilings, broken-pipe signalling with no readers, missed wakeups without ordering, and directory removal across lock upgrade requiring revalidation.
